---
title: "Windows: install Ubuntu; Mac: open Terminal"
---

We will use a **terminal** to give the computer short written instructions.
On Windows we use Ubuntu, a version of Linux, through **Windows Subsystem for
Linux (WSL)**. Mac users can use the Terminal application already on their Mac.

You do not need to understand the commands yet. This page gets you ready for
the first exercises. Installation help will be provided during the course.

## Windows: install Ubuntu

### 1. Prepare

Save your work: installation may require restarting your computer. You need an
internet connection and permission to install software. On a university-managed
computer, ask the teaching team if administrator access is unavailable.

Use Windows 11 for this setup. Microsoft's installation command also supports
Windows 10 version 2004 (build 19041) or later; if you have an older system,
ask for help choosing a supported course environment.

### 2. Open PowerShell as administrator

Open **Start**, type **PowerShell**, right-click **Windows PowerShell**, and
choose **Run as administrator**. Accept the Windows permission prompt.

PowerShell is a Windows command window. We use it for installation; later
Linux exercises belong in Ubuntu.

### 3. Install

In **PowerShell**, type this command and press **Enter**:

```powershell
wsl --install -d Ubuntu
```

Wait for it to finish and restart the computer if requested. This installs
Ubuntu alongside your Windows applications using WSL.

These steps follow [Microsoft's WSL installation instructions](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/wsl/install).

### 4. Open Ubuntu and create your Linux account

After restarting, open **Start**, search for **Ubuntu**, and open it. First
startup may take a little time.

When asked, choose a Linux username, for example `anna`, using lowercase letters.
Then choose a password and enter it again when prompted. This is a separate
account from your Windows account.

**Nothing appears while you type the password, not even dots.** This is normal.
Type it and press Enter. Keep the password somewhere secure; do not send it to
a teacher or include it in a screenshot.

When setup finishes, you should see a line ending in a prompt, often `$`.
The prompt means Ubuntu is waiting for a command. Do not type the `$` itself.

The account and password behaviour is described in
[Microsoft's environment setup guide](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/wsl/setup/environment).

### 5. Check Ubuntu

In **Ubuntu**, run these commands one at a time:

```bash
whoami
pwd
uname -s
```

`whoami` should show your Linux username. `pwd` shows your current folder,
usually `/home/` followed by your username. `uname -s` should print `Linux`.

To check WSL itself, open **PowerShell** and run:

```powershell
wsl --list --verbose
```

Look for an Ubuntu entry with `2` in the VERSION column. A running or stopped
state is normal. If your installation shows version 1, bring it to the setup
session so we can help check it.

### 6. Opening Ubuntu next time

Open **Ubuntu** from Start. You normally do not need administrator mode for
course exercises. Closing its window does not delete your saved files.

## Mac: use Terminal directly

Open **Finder**, then **Applications → Utilities → Terminal**. You can also
search for Terminal with Spotlight. You do not need to install Ubuntu.

Run the same three commands:

```bash
whoami
pwd
uname -s
```

Your home folder is usually `/Users/` followed by your username, and `uname -s`
prints `Darwin`, the underlying macOS system. That is expected. macOS is not
Linux, but the basic commands we use work in both environments. A prompt ending
in `%` is also normal on a Mac.

Commands labelled **Ubuntu only**, such as `apt`, do not belong in Mac Terminal.

## First exercise: a folder you can find again

On Windows use **Ubuntu**; on Mac use **Terminal**. Run one line at a time:

```bash
cd
mkdir -p introcomputing/first-session
cd introcomputing/first-session
pwd
ls
```

- `cd` on its own takes you to your home folder.
- `mkdir -p` creates the named folders if they do not already exist.
- `cd introcomputing/first-session` moves into that folder.
- `pwd` prints its full location, called its **path**.
- `ls` lists what is inside. A new, empty folder produces no listed filenames.

Now see the **same folder** in a graphical file manager:

**Windows — run in Ubuntu:**

```bash
explorer.exe .
```

**Mac — run in Terminal:**

```bash
open .
```

The dot means “the folder I am in now”. The file-manager window and the terminal
are showing the same place in two different ways.

Close the terminal, reopen it, and find your folder again:

```bash
cd ~/introcomputing/first-session
pwd
```

Here `~` is shorthand for your home folder. Being able to return to saved work
is part of being ready, even when the folder is still empty.

## Windows and Ubuntu have different home folders

On Windows, Ubuntu's `/home/anna` is different from Windows' `C:\Users\anna`.
A file downloaded by your Windows browser does not automatically appear in your
Ubuntu home folder. For terminal exercises, use the Ubuntu home folder we just
created. We will practise locating downloads and transferring files together.

You can reach Ubuntu files through `explorer.exe .`, or by entering `\\wsl$`
in File Explorer's address bar and opening your Ubuntu distribution.
See [Microsoft's guide to Windows and Linux file systems](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/wsl/filesystems).

R and RStudio will have separate setup instructions. You do not need to install
them inside Ubuntu to complete this page.

## If something goes wrong

| What you see | What to do |
| --- | --- |
| Windows asks for an administrator password you do not have | Ask the teaching team or the computer's administrator. |
| Installation appears stuck at 0% | In administrator PowerShell, try `wsl --install --web-download -d Ubuntu`, as described in Microsoft's installation guide. |
| A message mentions virtualisation or an optional component | Save the exact error and ask for setup help; settings may need an administrator. |
| Password typing appears to do nothing | No visible characters is normal. Type the password and press Enter. |
| `explorer.exe` is not found | Check that you are in Ubuntu on Windows. On Mac use `open .`; on a remote computer neither command is the course file-transfer method. |
| A Linux command gives an unexpected PowerShell error | Open Ubuntu from Start and try there. |

Bring the error message and the step you reached to the setup session. If local
installation is unavailable, we will help you use the course's
[remote Linux environment](remote-linux.qmd); connection details will follow.

## Ready for the first session

You can open the correct terminal, run `pwd`, create a folder, view that folder
in a file manager, and return to it after reopening the terminal. You do not
need to memorise the commands yet.
